CHAPTER 8  ·  THE APPENDICULAR SKELETON 
Study Guide  ·  Page 1 of 2 
130 appendicular bones of 210  ·  Most of them are in the hands and feet 
Front  ·  Pectoral Girdle & Upper Limb 
Learning goals.  Identify the bones.   Describe the major markings.   Palpate them.   Assess the Q angle. 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
Limbs + the girdles that hang them on the trunk. Only bony joint of the upper limb to the axial skeleton is clavicle ↔ manubrium; 
scapulae float on muscle. Pelvic girdle mixes axial bone (sacrum + coccyx) with two os coxae. Counts: pectoral girdle 4 · upper limbs 60 
· os coxae 2 · lower limbs 64 (including 4 foot sesamoids). 
 
PECTORAL GIRDLE 
 
Bone 
What to know 
Clavicle 
S-shaped. Sternal end thick/triangular; acromial end flattened — use that plus the curve to side a loose bone. 
Only upper-limb bone that meets the axial skeleton. 
Scapula 
Flat triangle over the posterior ribs, muscle-held, slides up-down and side-to-side for arm reach. Three borders 
(superior, medial, lateral) and three angles (superior, inferior, lateral). 
Spine & fossae 
Spine splits supraspinous fossa (above) from larger infraspinous fossa (below). Anterior face = subscapular 
fossa. Suprascapular notch sits on the superior border. 
Glenoid side 
Glenoid cavity = shallow socket for the humeral head. Acromion + coracoid wrap the head from above; 
acromion meets the clavicle at the top of the shoulder. 
Palpate: whole clavicle, jugular notch, acromion bump (also found by lifting the arm and feeling in the deltoid hollow). Retract the 
scapulae to see medial/lateral borders, inferior angle, and spine; coracoid may show on the upper chest just below the clavicle. 
 
ARM  —  humerus 
 
Marking 
Role 
Head / necks 
Head = ball of the glenohumeral joint. Anatomical neck = joint margin (synovial cavity). Surgical neck = 
narrow shaft just distal — common fracture site. 
Tubercles / deltoid 
tuberosity 
Greater and lesser tubercles = proximal rotator-cuff attachments. Mid-shaft deltoid tuberosity = deltoid 
insertion (sometimes felt with the arm partly flexed). 
Epicondyles & fossae 
Medial/lateral epicondyles stabilize the elbow (easy to feel). Posterior olecranon fossa takes the ulna in 
full extension. Anterior coronoid and radial fossae take ulna and radial head in full flexion. 
Capitulum / trochlea 
Capitulum (lateral) ↔ radial head. Trochlea (medial) ↔ ulna. Remember: capitulum is the “little head” 
for the radius. 
 
FOREARM  —  ulna & radius 
 
Ulna drives elbow motion and is large proximally; radius drives the hand and is large distally. They meet at both ends (proximal and 
distal radioulnar joints). Radius spins around the ulnar head in pronation / supination. 
Marking 
What it does 
Olecranon + trochlear notch Point of the elbow. Locks full extension and blocks overextension. Notch rotates on the humeral 
trochlea (hinge). 
Coronoid process 
Opposite the olecranon; seats in the humeral coronoid fossa in full flexion. 
Distal ulna 
Ulnar head meets the ulnar notch of the radius. Ulnar styloid = bump on the pinky side of the wrist. 
Ulna can be traced end-to-end. 
Radius 
Head spins on the capitulum and in the radial notch of the ulna. Radial tuberosity is a proximal muscle 
attachment. Radial styloid = bump on the thumb side of the wrist. Shaft is harder to feel than the ulna. 
 
WRIST & HAND  —  27 bones each side 
 
Mnemonic (thumb-side → pinky, proximal then distal):  So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb = scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, 
pisiform / hamate, capitate, trapezoid, trapezium. 
Group 
Details 
Proximal carpals 
Pisiform = bump just distal to the ulnar styloid. Triquetrum = bump at the base of the hypothenar 
eminence. Other carpals can be felt but are hard to name one-by-one. 
Distal carpals 
Hamate → ring + pinky. Capitate → middle. Trapezoid → index. Trapezium → thumb. 
Metacarpals + phalanges Metacarpal heads = knuckles. Dorsal lines on the hand are extensor tendons, not bone. Thumb has 2 
phalanges; fingers have 3. All 14 phalanges can be felt. 
 
JOINT PAIRINGS  ·  MOTION  ·  HOW TO SIDE A BONE 
 
What fits into what 
•  Olecranon ↔ olecranon fossa (full extension). 
•  Coronoid process ↔ coronoid fossa (full flexion). 
•  Radial head ↔ radial fossa (full flexion) and capitulum. 
•  Trochlear notch ↔ trochlea (hinge: flex/extend). 
•  Radial head spins on ulnar head (rotation: pronate/supinate). 
Carrying angle 
About 10–15° of valgus at the extended elbow. It lets the 
forearms clear the hips when the arms hang. 
 Left vs right in lab 
•  Clavicle: hold the S-curve so the flat acromial end is lateral 
and the thick triangular sternal end is medial; the conoid tubercle 
faces inferior/posterior. 
•  Scapula: glenoid faces lateral; spine is posterior; inferior angle 
points down. 
•  Humerus: head is medial/proximal; olecranon fossa is 
posterior; capitulum is lateral. 
•  Ulna: olecranon is proximal/posterior; styloid is distal; trochlear 
notch opens anterior. 
•  Radius: round head is proximal; styloid is distal and on the 
thumb side.

CHAPTER 8  ·  THE APPENDICULAR SKELETON 
Study Guide  ·  Page 2 of 2 
Q angle ≈ 8–10° males / 10–15° females  ·  Carrying angle ≈ 10–15° 
Back  ·  Pelvis, Lower Limb & Lab 
PELVIC GIRDLE 
 
Each os coxae = ilium + ischium + pubis fused. Meet at the pubic symphysis and at the sacrum. All three bones form the acetabulum. 
Ischium + pubis enclose the obturator foramen. Ischial rami = “sitz bones.” Inguinal ligament runs ASIS → pubic crest (easier to see on 
men). 
Feature 
What to know 
Ilium / crest 
Largest of the three. Crest = hands-on-hips ridge. Four spines: ASIS, AIIS, PSIS, PIIS. ASIS is a visible 
anterior bump; PSIS = dimples beside the sacrum. Auricular surface meets the sacrum. 
Ischium / pubis 
Ischium is posteroinferior. Pubic crest sits above the symphysis (easier on men; mons pubis often hides it). 
Ischial tuberosity takes sitting weight. 
Pelvic brim / inlet 
Sacral promontory + arcuate lines. Female brim is wider; whole female pelvis is wider and shorter so the 
hips are the widest part of the female body. 
Sciatic notches 
Greater notch passes the sciatic nerve into the leg; lesser notch passes other neurovascular structures. 
 
THIGH  —  femur & patella 
 
Largest, heaviest bone. Head + acetabulum = hip (fovea capitis on the head is a ligament attachment). Neck angles medially ~125° 
(angle of inclination), so the shaft is not in line with the tibia — that creates the Q angle. 
Marking 
Role 
Trochanters 
Greater = abductors (palpate on the side of the hip; easier if you swing the leg). Lesser = adductors and 
flexors. Intertrochanteric line/crest connect them. 
Shaft / condyles 
Linea aspera on the posterior shaft. Distal condyles meet the tibia; epicondyles above them are felt high 
on each side of the knee (best with the knee flexed). 
Patella 
Sesamoid in the quadriceps tendon. Tracks with flexion/extension and lengthens the quads’ lever arm. 
 
Q angle — required lab skill.  Angle between ASIS → mid-patella and tibial tuberosity → mid-patella. Pulls the knees inward so 
mass sits under the trunk. Wider female hips → larger Q (~10–15° vs ~8–10° in males). Measure supine: goniometer fulcrum on the 
patella, stationary arm to the tibial tuberosity, moving arm to ASIS. 
 
LEG  —  tibia & fibula 
 
Bone 
What to know 
Tibia 
Weight path: femur → tibia → ankle. Proximal condyles take the femoral condyles. Tibial tuberosity = patellar 
tendon (kicking). Anterior margin = shin. Distal medial malleolus = inner “ankle bone.” Felt end-to-end. 
Fibula 
Muscle anchor, not a main weight bone. Head meets the tibia under the lateral tibial condyle (same level as the 
tibial tuberosity). Distal lateral malleolus = outer “ankle bone,” and it sits lower than the medial one. 
Feet apart: flesh looks like an apex-up triangle, but the bones form a rectangle (easy stance). Feet together: flesh and bones both make 
an apex-down triangle (harder to stand). 
 
ANKLE & FOOT 
 
Walking weight path:  femur → tibia → talus → calcaneus → lateral foot / 5th metatarsal → metatarsal heads → hallux, which 
launches the next step. 
Sesamoids and the 206 count.  Each foot has two sesamoid bones under the hallux. Those four bones are the ones often not 
counted, so most sources list the adult skeleton as 206 bones rather than 210. 
Group 
Bones 
Hindfoot 
Talus (tibia sits on it) + calcaneus (heel). 
Midfoot 
Navicular (talus → three cuneiforms) + medial, intermediate, lateral cuneiforms + cuboid (calcaneus → 5th 
metatarsal). Highest point of the foot ≈ base of the 2nd metatarsal. 
Forefoot 
5 metatarsals + 14 phalanges. Hallux has 2 (IP). Other toes have 3 (PIP + DIP). 
Arches 
Medial longitudinal (keystone ≈ talus). Lateral longitudinal (keystone ≈ cuboid). Transverse (keystone ≈ 
medial cuneiform / 2nd metatarsal base). Ligament shock-absorbers; long ligaments → fallen arch. Shoes 
are implicated; barefoot walking can rebuild a weak arch. 
 
PALPATE  ·  LAB NUMBERS  ·  FETAL NOTES 
 
Feel these 
•  Clavicle end-to-end, acromion, both humeral epicondyles. 
•  Ulna end-to-end (olecranon → ulnar head/styloid). Radial head 
(spins in pronation) + radial styloid. 
•  Pisiform and triquetrum; knuckles; all phalanges. 
•  Iliac crest, ASIS, PSIS dimples, pubic crest, ischial ramus. 
•  Greater trochanter, femoral epicondyles, patella. 
•  Tibial condyles and tuberosity, entire shin, both malleoli, fibular 
head. 
•  Calcaneus, navicular on the medial arch, 5th-metatarsal 
tuberosity halfway heel-to-pinky. Coccyx just above the anus. 
 Lab numbers & extras 
•  Q angle: ~8–10° males, ~10–15° females. 
•  Carrying angle: ~10–15° at the elbow. 
•  Arch TAI: high <0.74 · normal 0.75–1.25 · low 1.26–2 · flat >2. 
Also record navicular height from the floor. 
•  Skeleton race: side every bone correctly; 10 seconds added 
per miss. 
Fetal skeleton 
Newborn ≈ 275 bones; many fuse to 210. Skull and ribcage large, 
limbs short, wrist/ankle mostly cartilage. Nearly straight mandible 
reduces bite leverage for nursing. Fontanels (“soft spots”) let the 
skull compress through the birth canal and last for months after 
birth.
